DXpmm1Hj3yO.content:
If a recipe tells you to sauté onions and garlic together for the same amount of time, ignore it!

Onions need time to soften and brown, but garlic cooks incredibly quickly and if it burns, it turns bitter.

Instead, sauté the onions first until they are softened (5ish mins), THEN add the garlic, and sauté for only 30 seconds to a minute. You’ll know it’s good to go when it becomes fragrant.

Then add any other ingredients your recipe calls for!￼

Exception to the rule is if the onions and garlic cook at a very low heat and they are stirred very frequently. Even then, I still would separate them out.￼

DX6ygxjDvl2.content:
Did you know that the majority (~70%) of SNAP recipients work full time (which is defined as a *minimum* of 35 hours a week)?

So maybe instead of arguing about whether they are “worthy” of prepared foods like rotisserie chicken, we should stop providing corporate welfare for their employers who don’t pay them enough to buy food to survive?

So many people who critique SNAP are quick to say that people are “lazy” or “they should get a job.” But this doesn’t tell the whole story - or even the majority of the story. Because the vast overall issue is underpayment and greed. I don’t really want my tax money to supplement bosses who either hoard money for themselves through greed or can’t handle running their businesses in an ethical and sustainable way resulting in not paying their employees enough to survive.

DW2H_40Ceb7.content:
Unpopular Opinion: You SHOULDN’T wash your chicken! 🙅🏼‍♀️

Rinsing raw chicken just splashes bacteria around your sink, counters, dishes… you. 🤢 It increases the risk for cross contamination and does NOTHING to improve the texture, flavor, or moisture content.

The only thing that will kill bacteria is HEAT!

To properly and safely cook your chicken:
Pat dry, season or marinate, and cook until your chicken reaches an internal temp of 165°F 🌡️

If you don’t want to spend the rest of your night sanitizing the entire kitchen, DON’T WASH YOUR CHICKEN ❌

DXaWoATDAp5.content:
Pickle dip is all over our feed right now but most recipes cost an arm and a leg to make! Today, we’re making it for just $7. 👏 Turns out you don’t need fancy pickles to make it slap. 🥒😎

Grab the full recipe below!

#budgetbytes #pickledip #budgetsnacks #viralrecipe #easyappetizer

Ingredients
8 oz cream cheese, softened
1/2 cup sour cream
1 cup finely chopped dill pickles
1 cup shredded cheddar 
2-3 tbsp pickle juice
1/2 tsp garlic powder
1/2 tsp onion powder
1 tsp dried dill 
Black pepper

Instructions:
1.) In a medium bowl, mix cream cheese and sour cream until smooth
2.) Stir in chopped pickles, shredded cheddar, pickle juice, garlic powder, onion powder, dill and black pepper
3.) Taste and adjust with more pickle juice if needed.
4.) Chill 30 minutes for best flavor

DYVe1v2pTTf.content:
Sometimes you just need to eat a whole cabbage. 🥬Cabbage is having its moment as the veggie of the year and honestly, we get it. It’s naturally affordable, incredibly versatile, and when you make it like THIS? Absolutely addictive. Toasted sesame oil, grated garlic, ground sesame seeds, and a little chicken powder is all it takes to make a bowl you will NOT stop eating. 
Here’s the full recipe:

Addictive Cabbage
½ large head green cabbage, cubed
2 Tbsp toasted sesame seeds, ground
3 cloves garlic, grated
1½ tsp chicken powder
½ tsp salt
2 Tbsp toasted sesame oil

Wash and dry cabbage, then cut into bite-sized cubes. Grind sesame seeds until sandy. Add everything to a bowl, toss, and lightly squeeze once or twice to help absorb the seasoning. Taste and adjust salt as needed. That’s it!

DWNEQMogCLU.content:
Spring produce may ~almost~ be upon us, but it's not too late to enjoy the flavors of winter produce in a hearty salad. 💪 Try this FoodPrints French Lentil Salad for an easy and fresh weekday lunch! 

Starting with a base of cooked French lentils, crunchy celery, and sweet dried apples, this salad is finished with a zippy lemon dressing that just gets better with time. 💚

Save the recipe at the link in our bio! 🔗

INGREDIENTS: 
1 cup French lentils (small green lentils, also called Le Puy)
4 cups water
1/4 cup olive oil
2 tablespoons lemon juice
salt and pepper to taste
3/4 cup dried apples, chopped
3/4 cup toasted sunflower seeds
3/4 cup celery, finely chopped

DIRECTIONS: 
1. Gather all the ingredients and equipment. Wash the produce and prepare it as detailed in the ingredients list. When rinsing and draining the lentils, look them over carefully for any small stones.
2. Place the lentils in a pot with the water over medium heat, bring them to a simmer and then reduce heat to low. Cook covered with a lid checking them often to avoid over-cooking.
3. Meanwhile, whisk together the olive oil, lemon juice, salt and pepper. Taste and adjust as needed.
4. When the lentils are tender (but not mushy), drain and toss with the dressing and remaining ingredients.
5. Chill salad for at least 30 minutes before serving.

🌱 Ramps are here! 🌱 Ramps are here! 🌱

For a few short weeks each spring, these wild alliums pop up across the Mid-Atlantic, bringing their signature garlicky-onion flavor to market tables. Foraged locally and highly seasonal, ramps are a true taste of spring that doesn't stick around for long!

❓What is foraging?
Foraging is the practice of harvesting food directly from the wild, rather than growing it intentionally. In the Mid-Atlantic, that often means gathering edible plants like ramps, mushrooms, or more from forests, fields, and other natural landscapes.

With ramps, foraging is especially common because they grow naturally in wooded areas with rich, moist soil, conditions that are hard to replicate at scale on farms. Experienced foragers know where to find them and how to harvest carefully, often taking only part of a patch (like a single leaf or a portion of the bulb) so the plants can regenerate year after year.

DXT5JGNIG91.content:
🌱 Spring is in full swing, which means one of the most anticipated vegetables has returned to market: asparagus! These fast-growing shoots quickly populate seasonal menus and are a mainstay in springtime cooking.

We caught up with asparagus expert Dana Garner Boyle of @garnersproduce to understand how they grow and reach our tables.

"Here at Garner's, we grow approximately 4 acres of asparagus, with varieties including Jersey Night, Millennium, and Purple Passion. We chose these varieties because they grow and perform well in our growing zone — they are high-yielding with great flavor and tenderness," Dana told us.

Asparagus is a perennial plant with a root system that winters over each year, called a crown. Planting is done in spring by digging furrows about 8 inches deep and laying crowns along the bottom with about a foot of space between plants. "Asparagus rows should be no closer than 3 feet apart," Dana explains. "After the roots are laid in the furrow, they should be covered immediately with 2 to 3 inches of soil," with the trench gradually filled as spears grow into ferns throughout the season.

Because the crown supplies vital nutrients to the shoots, growers must avoid over-harvesting. "Newly planted asparagus should only be harvested for one week in its first cutting year. Once established, we cut for 3 to 4 weeks in the second season, and up to 6 to 8 weeks in following years." This explains the short window we have to enjoy this spring treat! "An asparagus field can produce for 15 to 20 years if conditions are favorable," Dana adds.

Looking for an easy way to prepare these tender spears? Head to the link in bio for a simple FoodPrints recipe for roasted asparagus.

📍Find asparagus from your favorite local vegetable farmer in the coming weeks, or find Garner's Produce at Cleveland Park or Dupont Circle.

🌎 What does Earth Month look like at FoodPrints? It looks like this.

Last week, during DCPS spring break, our team came together for four days to completely rebuild the Ludlow-Taylor Elementary school garden — one of our biggest, with 960 square feet of growing space, first constructed back in 2017.

After years of use, the original beds were rotting and needed to be replaced. So our garden team planned every measurement, ordered the lumber, set up a full construction area behind the school, sawed wood to size, assembled raised beds, and hauled a five-foot pile of soil and compost — one wheelbarrow-load at a time — for the new beds to grow many fruit and veggie plants, including strawberries, blackberries, and asparagus.

More than 160 hours of work. Dozens of hands. Coordination with the Ludlow-Taylor PTO. FoodPrints teachers and admin team members. FRESHFARM market staff and volunteers. All showed up and worked hard during an unusually warm week.

"Even though it was hot and the project was a bit daunting in scale, with careful planning, many hands, and persistence, we accomplished this very large project together," notes Beth Bacon, FRESHFARM Education Director. "Now, in this flagship school garden, the beds will be stable and safe for students and will continue to grow many crops year-round for them to learn from, harvest, and eat."

FoodPrints staff put their hearts into their work every day, bringing joyful, hands-on experiences growing, cooking, and eating food together to thousands of Washington, DC, public elementary students each school year. But this project was particularly heartfelt, honoring the memory of Barbara Percival, one of FoodPrints' founders and first teachers, who tended this garden with so much love for so many years. 🫶🏽

DXl6tNUGS7H.content:
Ramps are almost gone! Many farmers are done foraging for the season, but we confirmed that @chicanoSol still has some (find them at Dupont Circle this Sunday). 

Grab the last of the season to make this versatile okonomiyaki. Okonomiyaki is a savory Japanese pancake traditionally made of flour, meat, cabbage, and other ingredients, cooked on a griddle and topped with various condiments. 

This 🌱 RAMP okonomiyaki features ramps, Brussels sprouts, and carrots, making it the perfect dish to bridge from winter veggies to the first tender crops of spring. 

Okonomiyaki are designed to be flexible, so feel free to throw in whatever crunchy veggies are lingering in your fridge (the season's first asparagus would be a welcome addition!) along with the ramps that give it a garlicky, springy kick.

(Special thanks to @alysekstokes, who developed and submitted this recipe!) 

Save this recipe at the LINK IN OUR BIO! 🔗

INGREDIENTS:
- 2 eggs
- 75g all purpose flour (about ⅔ cup)
- 75ml water (about ⅓ cup)
- a generous pinch of kosher salt
- 1 bunch ramps, chopped with a few greens set aside for garnish
- 1 cup shredded Brussels sprouts
- ½ cup shredded or shaved carrots
- 2 tsp neutral cooking oil

DIRECTIONS:
1. Place the eggs, flour, water, and salt in a medium bowl and whisk until there are no lumps remaining. You should have a smooth batter with the consistency of heavy cream.
2. Add the ramps, Brussels sprouts, and carrots. Using a rubber spatula, fold the veggies into the batter until well coated.
3. Heat the oil in a 10” nonstick pan over medium-high heat. Pour the batter into the pan, pressing to help evenly distribute the veggies. 
4. Cook for 3-4 minutes or until lightly browned on the first side. (You can gently lift the edge of the pancake with your spatula and peek underneath to confirm.)
5. Carefully flip the okonomiyaki over and cook on the other side for 2-3 more minutes, or until light golden brown.
6. Slide the finished okonomiyaki onto a plate and drizzle with your choice of sauces. Scatter the reserved ramp greens over the top to garnish.

If you’ve ever stood at a farmers market wondering when to show up, what’s actually a good deal, or how people seem to know exactly what to buy, this is worth a read.

The Washington Post just published a guide to being a smarter farmers market shopper, featuring experts from across the country, including Cat Oakar, Executive Director of FRESHFARM. (And if the images and videos look familiar, that’s because most of them were captured at FRESHFARM Arlington Market!)

It covers the basics people tend to learn the hard way: go early if you want full selection, later if you’re hoping for deals, and always do a lap before you commit. It also gets into the less obvious stuff, like how to think about pricing in a way that reflects what it actually takes to grow food and why “imperfect” produce is often the best value.

The best piece of advice? Talk to your farmers and producers. Ask what’s tasting best that day, what’s just come in, or what they’d take home themselves. That back-and-forth is where much of the value of market shopping actually lives.

There’s more in the full piece, and it’s a good one to bookmark heading into peak season. Thank you, @_karaelder, for the thoughtful and thorough reporting! Read the full story at the LINK IN OUR BIO!

DYHZCXrIGcx.content:
It's MOREL TIME! 🍄‍🟫

🌱Spring in the Mid-Atlantic brings a handful of highly anticipated seasonal foods, and for mushroom lovers, few are more exciting than MORELS. These wild mushrooms are known for their honeycomb-like caps, earthy flavor, and extremely short growing season. If you spot them at market this month, don’t wait too long, they may disappear just as quickly as they arrived.

This season, we’re excited to welcome @manchesterfungi to the FRESHFARM network. While the farm specializes in cultivated mushrooms year-round, managing partner Iain Davis notes that they bring foraged morels to market each spring.

“Morels are notoriously difficult to grow as they usually form symbiotic relationships with trees,” Davis explains. “They appear for a very short window each year, and while certain species can be more present, they remain rare.”

In the Mid-Atlantic, morels are often found in deciduous hardwood forests near dying elm, ash, and apple trees. Old orchards can be especially productive spots for experienced foragers. Their arrival typically coincides with warming spring soil temperatures around 50 degrees.

If you bring some home from market, Davis recommends soaking morels briefly in salted water before cooking. “Simply sauté them in butter and garlic until they begin to get crispy, then season with salt and pepper,” he says. “Being from Maryland, we also love to add Old Bay!”

DYPwhsDE5Wh.content:
Not sure what to do with the asparagus you picked up at market? 💚 This vibrant soup celebrates a seasonal favorite at its peak. Silky smooth, it comes together in under an hour and tastes like pure spring!

Save this recipe at the link IN OUR BIO!

INGREDIENTS:
- 3 lbs asparagus
- 2 leeks, white and light green parts only, or 1 large onion, chopped
- 2 sprigs of green garlic, or 3 cloves of garlic
- 4 tablespoons butter, divided
- ¾ teaspoon salt, plus more as needed
- ½ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper
- 4 cups chicken or vegetable stock
- ¼ cup chopped fresh parsley (optional)
- 1 cup heavy cream, plus more for garnish (optional)
- ½ cup chopped fresh tender herbs, such as dill or chive
- Garnish: reserved asparagus tips, chopped herbs, heavy cream

DIRECTIONS: 
1. Soak the asparagus in a large bowl of water with the tips facing down to dislodge any sand and soil. Remove, rinse thoroughly, and snap off the woody ends. Chop into 1-inch pieces, reserving about ⅓ of the tips.
2. If using leeks, soak them in a bowl of water after chopping to dislodge any dirt.
3. Roughly chop the green garlic or garlic cloves.
4. In a large stockpot, melt 1 tablespoon of butter over medium heat. Add the reserved asparagus tips, sprinkle with a pinch of salt, and sauté for about 5 minutes, until bright green and tender-crisp. Set aside.
5. Melt the remaining butter in the same pot. Add the leeks or onion, ¾ teaspoon salt, and pepper, and sauté until softened, 8 to 10 minutes. Add the garlic and chopped asparagus and sauté for about 5 minutes, stirring occasionally.
6. Add the stock, bring to a boil, then reduce the heat to low and simmer uncovered for 15 to 20 minutes. Stir in the parsley, if using—it will brighten the finished soup’s color.
7. Using an immersion blender or a standard blender, blend the soup until smooth. If using a standard blender, let the soup cool slightly, then blend in batches, venting the lid to allow steam to escape. Return the soup to the pot, stir in the heavy cream if using, and gently reheat.
8. Ladle into bowls and serve topped with a drizzle of heavy cream, fresh herbs, and the reserved asparagus tips.

DYZamzZko4B.content:
@twinspringsfruitfarm has been growing in the rolling hills of Adams County, Pennsylvania since 1979. Today, the family farm produces gorgeous fruit and vegetables for 20 Mid-Atlantic farmers markets, including one of spring’s most distinctive crops: rhubarb. 🩷

❓ Though often treated like a fruit in pies and jams, rhubarb is actually a perennial vegetable known for its tart flavor and multicolor stalks. In the Mid-Atlantic, rhubarb thrives in cooler spring temperatures and can stay productive year after year.

“We grow about an acre and a half of rhubarb,” shared Jesse King of Twin Springs Fruit Farm. “This year, we planted some newer red varieties because our shoppers want the rich red stalks." Rhubarb prefers well-drained soil, plenty of nutrients, and consistent weed management. “They do not like to have wet feet,” King said, noting that raised beds and compost-rich soil help keep plants healthy.

Unlike annual crops, rhubarb plants can take several years to become fully productive, but healthy crowns can continue yielding for 10 to 20 years with proper care. Growers also remove flower stalks throughout the season so the plants can direct energy back into foliage and root development for future harvests.

➡️ At the market, rhubarb’s short season makes it a spring favorite for recipes like our crisp bars, compote, or a simple crumble (with ice cream). Link in bio to explore our recipes. Shop for tender stalks and enjoy it while it lasts!

📍Find Twin Springs Fruit Farm at Arlington, Dupont Circle, and Mosaic.

DWDgDurksvA.content:
You’re not losing to the market.
You’re losing to your ego.

The harder you study investing,
the faster you might lose money.

Most people don’t lose because they don’t know enough.

They lose because they refuse to admit one thing:

“I’m wrong.”

In Think Again, Adam Grant talks about a real tragedy.

In 1949, a group of elite firefighters were trapped in a wildfire at Mann Gulch.

They had to run for their lives.

But many of them died.

Not because they were weak.
Not because they didn’t try.

But because they held onto their tools.

Axes. Saws. Heavy gear.

Even when every second mattered.

This isn’t about strength.

It’s about identity.

Under pressure,
those tools became who they were.

Letting go didn’t just mean running faster.

It meant:

“I’m no longer who I think I am.”

And here’s the uncomfortable truth:

You’ve done the same thing.

In the market,
that “heavy axe” is your losing trade.

You’ve seen it:

The setup is broken.
The direction is wrong.
The logic no longer holds.

But you stay.

Not because it makes sense.

But because closing it means:

“I was wrong.”

So you hold.

You hope.

You wait.

But you’re not protecting your trade.

You’re protecting your ego.

That’s how accounts slowly die.

The best traders aren’t always right.

They’re just faster at letting go of being right.

A stop loss isn’t failure.

It’s the price you pay to learn something new.

Try this:

Before every trade, write one sentence:

“If this happens, I’m wrong.”

Not vague.
Not emotional.
Clear.

Because if you don’t define what being wrong looks like—

You’re not investing.

You’re gambling.

The market doesn’t care how much you studied.

It doesn’t care how confident you feel.

It only cares about one thing:

Can you survive your mistakes?

I don’t teach people how to make money.

I teach them how not to die in the market.

Investing isn’t about becoming stronger.

It’s about surviving your own mistakes.

— Harvey
The trader who tells you to wash the cup first.

DWMBieDkoFG.content:
You don’t fail to cut losses because you’re emotional.

You fail because you never defined what “wrong” looks like.

—

Most people enter a trade with a plan for profit.

Targets.
Scenarios.
What they hope will happen.

But almost no one clearly defines:

“What would prove me wrong?”

So when things start to shift…

Price moves against you.
The setup weakens.
Momentum disappears.

You don’t act.

Not because you’re undisciplined.

But because there’s nothing to act on.

No line.
No trigger.
No definition.

Just feeling.

—

So you hesitate.

You wait.

You tell yourself:

“Maybe it will come back.”
“Maybe I just need more time.”

But what you’re really saying is:

“I never decided what being wrong means.”

—

And without that…

There is no stop loss.

Only a delayed reaction.

—

The market doesn’t punish mistakes.

It punishes undefined mistakes.

—

The difference between a trader who survives
and one who slowly disappears isn’t intelligence.

It’s clarity.

Before every trade, the real question isn’t:

“How much can I make?”

It’s:

“What exactly would prove me wrong?”

Not vague.
Not emotional.
Not “I’ll feel it.”

Clear.

Specific.

Decided in advance.

—

Because the moment you define what “wrong” looks like,

You remove the need to negotiate with yourself.

—

And most losses don’t come from being wrong.

They come from negotiating with reality
after you already are.

—

You don’t need more knowledge.

You need fewer undefined decisions.

—

That’s where most people break.

Not in the market.

But in the moment they refuse to define the truth.

—

I’m Harvey.

The trader who tells you to wash the cup first.

DWvW6iwEhBK.content:
You don’t keep changing strategies because you’re curious.
You do it because staying with one forces you to face yourself.
—
At first, it feels logical.
“This system doesn’t work.”
“I need something better.”
“Maybe I just haven’t found the right strategy yet.”
So you switch.

Again.
And again.
And again.
—
But if you look closely…
The result never really changes.
Different indicators.
Different setups.
Different rules.
Same outcome.
—
It’s not the strategy.
It’s what the strategy forces you to confront.

Because every system, no matter how good,
will eventually put you in a situation where:

You have to take a loss.
You have to be wrong.
You have to follow a rule you don’t feel like following.

And that’s the moment most people break.
Not because the system failed.
But because they did.

So instead of fixing that…
They switch.

To a new strategy.
A new framework.
A new “solution.”

—

Not to improve.
But to escape.

Because as long as it’s the strategy’s fault,
You never have to face your own patterns.

That’s why most traders don’t lack knowledge.
They lack consistency with discomfort.

The uncomfortable truth is:
If you can’t follow one system through losses,
You won’t follow any system long enough to succeed.

You don’t need a better strategy.
You need to stop running from the same problem.

—

I’m Harvey.
The trader who tells you to wash the cup first.

DOt5siRCVgQ.content: Emmy-winning editor Chris Kronus brought his talent to the “BZRK” short film. With a background in character-driven docs and shorts for Netflix, National Geographic and PBS, Chris was excited to work in a new-to-him genre, especially with such a passionate director. In collaborating with director Chandler Clarke, Chris gave form to the crushing anxieties that can define a troubled past. By varying the pacing of cuts, Chris aimed to disorient the audience and make them feel the friction between Anders’ simmering exterior and the collapsing of his inner world. We can’t wait for you to experience his vision on screen in the world of “BZRK.”

BkdIzUxA5oc.content:
It’s my best friend’s birthday! So please permit me a few words:

If you asked me to use one word to describe her, it might be “strong.” Sometimes I see people longing for more representation in media, more strong women characters, more strong women politicians, more strong women generally. And that is true. We do need that.

But strength is useless in and of itself. Strength without patience, strength without convictions, strength without determination is far less remarkable. But Lena has all of these things, and of course it doesn’t make her perfect - but this is her birthday and not a day to be nuanced and careful about my portrayal.

And Lena, at the same time, isn’t only her strength - sometimes she is silly, sometimes she is the best person to go to for advice, and sometimes she is the person you need to have an argument with.

Here’s to another year of her existence! Love you, bestie.

Brad’s posts center on everyday queer, geeky, and Denver life: selfies and outfit “realness,” books, Star Wars, Bowie, comics, friends, chosen family, birthdays, travel, and advocacy like Spirit Day, voting, and queer/disabled visibility. CfAkY8bo8bF.content:
Took the kids to DC for the weekend. Today, we stopped at the Freedmen House Museum of Alexandria which honors the lives and experiences of the enslaved and free Black people who lived in and were trafficked through Alexandria. On the last floor of the museum there is an exhibit that asks the observer to identify someone that should be recognized for contributing to African American history. Both children, independently of themselves and without influence from me, left cards with my name on it. 

I don't know if they understood what the exhibit was asking or the gravity of what they implied. But that they could experience so much history, in such vivid detail, and think of me as worthy of recognition is an indescribable feeling. Happy Father's Day. 

🙏🏾

DYCw-bWDdib.content:
AAANY was proud to attend the District 38 Labor Townhall at Sunset Park High School alongside community members, workers, organizers, and advocates committed to supporting working families across our communities. 

The discussion focused on labor issues, worker protections, organizing efforts, and the challenges many workers are currently facing, while creating space for community members to share experiences and explore collective solutions.

Thank you to Council Member Alexa Avilés and everyone involved in organizing this important event, as well as all community partners and volunteers who helped make these conversations possible.

Together, we continue building stronger, safer, and more empowered communities.

تفخر الجمعية العربية الأمريكية في نيويورك بحضور لقاء العمل المجتمعي الخاص بالحي 38 في Sunset Park High School، إلى جانب أعضاء المجتمع، والعمّال، والمنظمين، والمدافعين عن حقوق العمال، دعمًا للعائلات العاملة في مجتمعاتنا.

ركزت المناقشات على قضايا العمل، وحقوق وحماية العمال، وجهود التنظيم المجتمعي، والتحديات التي يواجهها العديد من العمال، مع توفير مساحة لأفراد المجتمع لمشاركة تجاربهم واستكشاف حلول جماعية.

شكرًا لعضوة مجلس المدينة Alexa Avilés ولكل من ساهم في تنظيم هذا اللقاء المهم، وكذلك لجميع الشركاء والمتطوعين الذين ساعدوا في إنجاح هذه الحوارات المجتمعية.
معًا، نواصل بناء مجتمعات أقوى وأكثر أمانًا وتمكينًا.

DYC-4c_kfso.content:
AAANY was proud to join thousands of workers, immigrants, organizers, unions, and community members at the May Day Rally with the New York Immigration Coalition (NYIC) in support of worker and immigrant rights across New York City. ✊🏽📣

This International Workers’ Day, communities came together to stand against injustice and uplift the power, dignity, and contributions of immigrant workers who keep our city moving every single day.

Together with 78 organizations and more than 20,000 New Yorkers in the streets, we marched in solidarity for safer communities, worker protections, immigrant rights, and a future built on justice and collective power.

Immigrant power. Worker power. Community power. Together, we are unstoppable. ❤️

تفخر الجمعية العربية الأميركية في نيويورك بمشاركتها إلى جانب آلاف العمال، والمهاجرين، والمنظمين، والنقابات، وأفراد المجتمع في مسيرة May Day بالتعاون مع New York Immigration Coalition (NYIC)، دعمًا لحقوق العمال والمهاجرين في مدينة نيويورك. ✊🏽📣

في يوم العمال العالمي، اجتمعت المجتمعات معًا رفضًا للظلم، وتأكيدًا على قوة وكرامة ومساهمات العمال المهاجرين الذين يواصلون دعم وتحريك مدينتنا كل يوم.

إلى جانب 78 منظمة وأكثر من 20 ألف شخص خرجوا إلى الشوارع، سرنا معًا تضامنًا من أجل مجتمعات أكثر أمانًا، وحقوق العمال، وحقوق المهاجرين، ومستقبل قائم على العدالة والقوة الجماعية.

قوة المهاجرين. قوة العمال. قوة المجتمع.
معًا نحن لا يمكن إيقافنا ❤️

AAANY’s youth programs visited Dear Laila, an immersive installation by Palestinian artist Basel Zaraa that explores memory, displacement, family, and the meaning of home through the eyes of a child. Through storytelling, sound, and reflection, our young people engaged in thoughtful conversations about heritage, belonging, resilience, and the experiences many immigrant and refugee communities carry across generations. ✨

Experiences like these create space for youth to connect with culture, history, identity, and one another while encouraging creativity, empathy, and self-expression.

Participants from AAANY’s youth programs are building safe, empowering spaces where young people can learn, grow, lead, and find community together. ✨

WASHINGTON, D.C., March 16, 2026 — The Embassy of Mongolia hosted diplomats, defense officials, and guests to mark Mongolian Military Day and the 105th anniversary of the modern Armed Forces.

The evening opened with national anthems and remarks from Colonel Gankhuyag Dorjderem, who reflected on Mongolia’s historic March 18, 1921 victory and its lasting role in shaping the nation’s Armed Forces. Today, Mongolia contributes actively to global peacekeeping, maintaining defense partnerships with over 40 countries and participating in missions worldwide.

U.S. defense representative Cynthia Carras highlighted continued cooperation between Mongolia and the United States, including joint training efforts like the Khaan Quest exercise and ongoing collaboration in UN peacekeeping missions.

In closing, Chargé d’Affaires Battushig Zanabazar noted that more than 25,000 Mongolian service members have contributed to international missions, underscoring Mongolia’s global role as a trusted partner.

The evening concluded with a cultural performance featuring the morin khuur and traditional throat singing, celebrating Mongolia’s rich heritage.

This is what building the pipeline actually looks like.

Howard University's Cathy Hughes School of Communications and Forbes have launched a partnership to diversify business and financial journalism from the inside. Announced during Black Press Week 2026 at the ForbesBLK 50: Money Masters panel, the program creates a direct pathway for Howard students to enter Forbes's newsroom as HBCU Scholars.

The initiative pairs a year-round curriculum in wealth reporting and economic analysis with a competitive summer internship, placing one selected scholar alongside veteran editors covering global leadership and entrepreneurship. It is built on a simple premise: Black journalists should not just be included in financial media. They should lead it.

As the Black press approaches its 200th anniversary, Howard and Forbes are making sure the next generation of voices is already in the room. LINK IN BIO!

Washington Performing Arts celebrated its diamond anniversary on March 22 at the Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Library, an evening that honored six decades of cultural enrichment with the energy the organization is known for. Ari Shapiro brought his signature wit, pianist Henry Kopersk commanded the keys, and the Children of the Gospel Choir reminded every person in the room why arts education matters.

The night raised more than $680,000 for arts education, world-class performances, and grassroots community programs. After the performances, the celebration moved to the dance floor, because sixty years of service to this city deserves more than a standing ovation.

Flowers do not simply decorate a room. They hold a conversation with it.

Art in Bloom DC returns for its sixth year, transforming the historic Anderson House into a living gallery where over 30 floral installations reinterpret Revolutionary War-era art and architecture. Laura Dowling, former White House florist, joins Sarah Campbell of Netflix's "The Big Flower Fight" and luxury educator Sarah Khan for a four-day exhibition that blurs the line between botanical design and fine art.

Each installation is an ephemeral sculpture, using texture, scent, and color to create a dialogue between centuries-old paintings and the fleeting beauty of the natural world. It is a celebration of cultural continuity, timed perfectly with DC's cherry blossom season and rooted in the same spirit of friendship that first brought those iconic trees to the capital.

Permanence and change, history and bloom. This is what DC does best. Link in Bio!

DW1hyy-kcqj.content:
Leadership is not taught in a lecture hall. It is practiced at the table.

Guy Djoken, Executive Director of the UNESCO Center for Peace, traveled across Colombia this month to bring the International Model United Nations STEAM Summer Program directly to students. From Universidad del Valle in Cali to Colegio San Viator and San Rafael in Bogota, the message was consistent: young people are not the future of diplomacy. They are the present.

The IMUN-STEAM program combines Model United Nations simulations with STEAM education, placing students in the role of international delegates tackling real global issues. Participants build public speaking, negotiation, and problem-solving skills while developing sustainable solutions aligned with the UN 2030 Agenda.

Previous participants have reported stronger leadership abilities, expanded global perspectives, and lasting international connections. This is what preparing agents of change looks like in practice.

#UNESCO  #CulturalDiplomacy #YouthLeadership #WashingtonDC #GlobalEducation

DW4GlpUEVhq.content:
Energy justice is not just about power grids. It is about who gets to participate in building them.

At the 70th session of the UN Commission on the Status of Women in New York, Guy Djoken joined international policymakers for a high-level side event: “Catalysing Energy Justice: Energising Communities Through Girls/Women and Sport.” The session addressed clean energy access as a tool for empowerment, connecting energy policy to education, economic opportunity, and health outcomes for women, youth, and underserved communities worldwide.

The event spotlighted the Girls in Energy Project, an initiative integrating clean energy with education, economic empowerment, and sports. Organized by the DoTheDream Youth Development Initiative, the conversation centered on mobilizing $20 million for scalable solutions across the Global South and positioning young women as leaders in sustainable energy systems.

Achieving energy justice requires not only innovation, but inclusion. This is what that looks like at the highest level.

#UNESCO #MyHometownMyLens #EnergyJustice #WashingtonDC #WomenInLeadership

DXFNgdYlPUV.content:
Diplomacy starts with showing up.

On March 27, global leaders, creatives, and young professionals filled the Ronald Reagan Building for WECAA's celebration of America's upcoming 250th anniversary. The Washington Educational and Cultural Attache Association brought together voices from diplomacy, culture, and community for one evening that made the case: international relationships are built through people, not just policy.

Ambassador Youssef Amrani was honored as Ambassador of the Year, recognizing Morocco's historic role as one of the first countries to recognize the United States. Representatives from Djibouti, Malaysia, Haiti, Denmark, Lebanon, and Costa Rica shared reflections on what America's 250th means from a global perspective.

The program moved from diplomacy to culture, with speakers from Events DC and Theatre Washington highlighting how art, fashion, music, and faith shape understanding between nations. The Trust for the National Mall described it as "America's front porch." The Adams Memorial Foundation shared plans to honor one of the country's founding families.

For young professionals in the room, this was more than a reception. It was a look at how the next generation shapes what comes next. Link in Bio!

A kimono is not simply worn. It is read.

The Embassy of Japan in Washington, D.C. opened its historic Old Residence to Cherry Blossom Program delegates for an evening that turned fabric into language. Kimono specialist Hideko Uchiyama guided the room through centuries of meaning woven into silk: various colors, patterns, and sleeve lengths correspond to specific seasons, social statuses, and formal occasions. Every fold carries intention.

Delegates did not just observe. They stepped into the tradition, trying on authentic kimono pieces and experiencing the elaborate layering and refined posture the garment demands. It was a lesson in diplomacy through dress, an exchange that honored 113 years of U.S.-Japan relations while cultivating a new generation of cultural advocates.

Some traditions are preserved in museums. Others are preserved by being passed from hand to hand.

DXcFHLVkaBY.content:
Three thousand trees. One hundred thirteen years. One avenue.

The National Cherry Blossom Festival parade returned to Constitution Avenue, carrying forward a tradition rooted in Japan's 1912 gift of 3,020 cherry trees to the United States. The gesture was years in the making. Travel writer Eliza Scidmore championed the cause for decades before First Lady Helen Herron Taft gave it the backing it needed. On March 27, 1912, Mrs. Taft and Viscountess Chinda planted the first two Yoshino trees at the Tidal Basin, a ceremony intended to serve as a symbol of the growing friendship and cultural bond between the two nations.

That bond was on full display. Marching bands, giant helium balloons, contemporary dancers, recording artists, traditional Japanese drummers, and performers in authentic kimono filled the parade route. It was spectacle and substance in equal measure, a public celebration that honors both the beauty of the bloom and the diplomacy behind it.

This is what a gift looks like a century later. Still growing. Still bringing people together.

Washington, D.C. hosts the largest celebration of Japanese culture in the United States.

The Sakura Matsuri Japanese Street Festival brings traditional taiko drumming, martial arts demonstrations, classical dance, anime culture, sake tastings, and kimono showcases to Pennsylvania Avenue every spring. One drop of water. One smartphone. One minute.

Researchers at Germany's Federal Institute for Materials Research and Testing have built a rapid contamination test that detects fecal contamination in water using a single drop, a 3D-printed smartphone attachment, and the phone's own camera.

The technology reads urobilin, a natural byproduct of hemoglobin breakdown that traces human or animal waste in water. It was validated on real river samples and at a Berlin wastewater treatment plant. It works in complex field conditions, no lab required, no 24-hour wait, no specialized equipment.

For the communities living without reliable clean water access, in disaster zones, in regions where a municipal testing system does not reach, this is what accessible public health looks like: diagnostics in your pocket.

Missing since 1931. Found in Chad, 94 years later.

The rusty bush lark, a small bird native to the Sahel, was photographed by two French birders in February 2026. It was the first confirmed sighting since 1931. The species, Calendulauda rufa, had gone quiet for nearly a century.

It was not gone.

The rediscovery joins a growing list of species recovered by citizen scientists, amateur birders, and field researchers working the quiet margins of conservation biology. "Missing" is not the same as "gone." The rusty bush lark reappeared because people kept looking.

Nature keeps its own records. Full story in bio!

The Trust for the National Mall reprised its Monumental Conversations series with a discussion on women's leadership in the United States Armed Forces. Navy veterans Naomi Slusser and Sarah Watson joined retired Army Captain Erica Jeffries Purdo on a panel moderated by Brittany Masalosalo, Chief Public Policy Officer at HP Inc.

The panelists shared firsthand accounts of the distinctive obstacles and accomplishments facing female service members, illustrating how women's leadership roles within the military have evolved over decades.

The conversation extended beyond personal narrative. The panel examined how the memorials on the National Mall represent military heritage and what those landmarks mean as America approaches its 250th anniversary on July 4, 2026.

Forty-six years of sovereignty. One evening of diplomacy.

The Zimbabwean Mission in Washington, D.C. hosted a commemorative celebration for Zimbabwe's 46th Independence anniversary, drawing approximately 100 guests from the diplomatic community, the business sector, and the Zimbabwean diaspora.

Ambassador David D. Hamadziripi delivered the keynote address under the theme "Zimbabwe at 46, Unity and Development Towards Vision 2030," emphasizing that economic diplomacy is a critical element of Zimbabwe's foreign policy strategy. The goal: upper-middle-income status by 2030.

Honorable Jason Grubb from the U.S. Department of State highlighted shared priorities in agriculture, tourism, mining, and technology, reinforcing the collaboration that continues to shape the bilateral relationship.

The evening also marked a shift for the local Democratic organization. Chair Charles Wilson and Raskin honored a new generation of political leaders prepared to carry forward the principles of civil rights and home rule.

DYmxXpqDako.content:
Mental health support should not be treated like a luxury.

DC teenagers are pushing for comprehensive support systems beyond traditional school counseling. Students are naming the pressure directly: anxiety, stress, burnout, and feeling unsupported in their emotional well-being.

The barriers are structural. Cost, wait times, and stigma keep young people from accessing care. Current discourse prioritizes discipline and academics while mental health gets treated as secondary.

What students are asking for is specific: more accessible counseling, safe spaces for after-school activities, mentorship programs, and community-centered support. Youth organizations are integrating mental health with housing, economic opportunity, and public safety, understanding that none of these issues exist in isolation.

The conversation is shifting. Social media and youth summits are normalizing what previous generations were taught to suppress. Policy groups are advocating for wellness investments over punishment-focused approaches.

DYpWKcJCs75.content:
The curfew debate is loud. The teenagers are louder.

Washington expanded curfew zones to Navy Yard and U Street this year. Officials framed it as a safety measure. Teenagers across the city responded with a different diagnosis: the problem is not what time young people are outside. The problem is that there is nowhere for them to go.

At the District's Teen Summit this spring, students spoke directly about mental health, stress, safety, and how disconnected they feel from the people making decisions about their lives. Large public gatherings, they explained, are often less about causing problems and more about finding connection in a city that can feel isolating.

Many neighborhoods lack consistent recreation spaces, youth-focused alternatives, or affordable activities. Advocates argue that investing in arts programs, mental health support, sports access, and career development would create a larger long-term impact than stricter enforcement.

Spaces, not curfews. That is what they are asking for.

✦ Echo Media | United Media Group

DY3BuqQAQ7E.content:
528 children are dead in Bangladesh. The world is barely paying attention.

Since mid-March, Bangladesh has recorded more than 60,000 measles cases. The disease has reached 58 of the country's 64 districts. Almost every victim is under five years old. On May 4 alone, 17 children died in a single day. Dr. William Moss of Johns Hopkins called it a massive outbreak with a lot of mortality.

Hospitals in Dhaka are overwhelmed and running out of intensive care beds. UNICEF has deployed teams. But the system is strained beyond its limit.

Measles is preventable. The vaccine exists. It costs less than 50 cents a dose and it works. The vaccination program that had been working for years became underfunded and irregular. And now 528 children are dead.

Hantavirus and Ebola get headlines every day. 528 dead children in Bangladesh are getting silence.

Follow @updatenow.ai -- news without the filter.
